title: Day ten after chemo
objective: Recognize fever in an immunocompromised or neutropenic patient as an emergency

brief.situation: 19:50 in the emergency department. You are the nurse in a single room. Ms. Novak, 44, is ten days after her second cycle of chemotherapy for breast cancer. She has felt shivery since the afternoon. Triage was at 19:30.
handover: Triage: ESI 2. Temperature 38.4 C, heart rate 108, blood pressure 112/70, SpO2 97%. Implanted port in the right chest.

The department's neutropenic fever pathway: a single room, two sets of blood cultures (one from the port), the ordered broad-spectrum IV antibiotic within 60 minutes of triage without waiting for the blood count, no rectal temperatures, and the physician called at once for hypotension or confusion.
The physician has seen her and is in the department.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time; study pace runs three simulated minutes per real minute. Pause any time.
Assess and treat as you think the patient needs. Each assessment takes the time on its button.
Partway through you are asked to write what you think is happening. A debrief scores what you did.

The physician called within 5 minutes of hypotension or confusion (department pathway).
The ordered antibiotic within 60 minutes of triage, 30 minutes after she reaches the room (department pathway).
A focused assessment or question: about 1 min.
About 10 minutes for the physician to start fluids and vasopressor planning and move her to intensive care; a ward bed about 10 minutes.

why.question: Ms. Novak is hypotensive and confused. What is happening, and what do you do?

parts.label: What is happening
parts.criteria: Fever ten days after chemotherapy is neutropenic fever until shown otherwise; hypotension, confusion and mottling are septic shock developing.
parts.modelAnswer: Fever ten days after chemotherapy is neutropenic fever. Now she's hypotensive, confused and mottled: septic shock is setting in.

parts.label: What I do
parts.criteria: Cultures and the antibiotic without waiting for the count (within 60 minutes of triage); fluid; physician now; no rectal temperatures; hand off.
parts.modelAnswer: Cultures and the antibiotic are in without waiting for the count, fluid is running, and I call the physician now and hand off the times.

scoring.modelReasoning: Fever ten days after chemotherapy is neutropenic fever until proven otherwise. Cultures (one from the port) and the ordered antibiotic go in within an hour of triage without waiting for the count; no rectal temperatures. When she becomes hypotensive and confused, septic shock is developing: the physician comes now.
